goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: | P2 | app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 | Concurrent validations can overwrite each other's match_count increment because the read-modify-save update is non-atomic. | correctness | 0.98 |

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in app/models/blocked_email.rb lines 12-16 a read-modify-save pattern: `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`. This is indeed non-atomic - if two concurrent requests check the same email, both could read the same match_count value, increment it locally, and save, resulting in only one increment being recorded instead of two. This is a real race condition bug in the new code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: | P1 | db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:3 | Reusing an existing migration version means deployed databases that already recorded it will never create blocked_emails. | data-migration | 0.99 |

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims the migration is 'reusing an existing migration version', but there's no evidence in the diff that this migration version (20130724201552) already exists. This is a new file being created (indicated by 'new file mode' in the diff header). The finding appears to be making an assumption about the state of the database that cannot be verified from the diff alone. The migration file is being added as a new file, which is the standard way to create migrations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: | P2 | db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:5 | action_type has no database default, so imports or writes that bypass validations fail the NOT NULL constraint despite the model-only default. | data-migration | 0.98 |

adjudication.rationale: The migration at db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb creates the action_type column with 'null: false' but no database-level default value. The model's set_defaults callback only sets action_type via before_validation, which means any direct database inserts, bulk imports, or operations that bypass ActiveRecord validations will fail the NOT NULL constraint. This is a real defect - the model default at line 22 of blocked_email.rb (self.action_type ||= BlockedEmail.actions[:block]) won't help if the database is accessed directly.

adjudication_records.issue_text: | P2 | app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 | Each email validation does a lookup and, for a blocked address, a synchronous counter update (with validation) on the signup request path. | performance | high |

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that BlockedEmail.should_block? (lines 11-18) performs a database lookup and, when a match is found, does a synchronous save with validation (record.save) on every email validation during signup. This is visible in the diff at app/models/blocked_email.rb lines 11-18. While this is a legitimate performance concern for the signup path (each blocked email check triggers a DB write with validation), it's not a bug per se - the code functions correctly. It's an architectural/performance concern that a reviewer might reasonably flag.

adjudication_records.issue_text: | P1 | app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 | Case-sensitive exact email lookup lets domain-case variants bypass a blocked-address rule. | security | high |

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows BlockedEmail.should_block? uses `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` which performs a case-sensitive lookup in most databases. Email addresses have case-insensitive local parts by convention and case-insensitive domains by RFC. An attacker could bypass a blocked email 'bad@spammer.org' by registering as 'bad@SPAMMER.org' or 'BAD@spammer.org'. The code doesn't normalize email case before lookup, making this a valid security bypass vulnerability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: | P2 | spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:10 | The new validator examples stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so no User-validation path proves a persisted blocked address rejects signup and increments its match statistics. | testing | high |

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the EmailValidator spec (lines 10-22) stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? rather than using real BlockedEmail records. This means there's no integration test proving that when a user signs up with a blocked email, the BlockedEmail.should_block? method actually increments match_count and updates last_match_at statistics. The BlockedEmail model spec tests should_block? in isolation, and the validator spec tests the validator with stubs, but there's no end-to-end test through User validation that exercises both together. This is a legitimate testing gap for newly added functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: | P2 | lib/validators/email_validator.rb:4 | No test covers the whitelist/blacklist branches moved out of `User`, leaving the existing domain-restriction behavior unprotected by this change. | testing | high |

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the whitelist/blacklist logic was moved from User model's email_validator method to the new EmailValidator class (lib/validators/email_validator.rb lines 4-11), but the new test file (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) only tests the BlockedEmail.should_block? functionality, not the whitelist/blacklist branches. The test file shows tests for 'blocked email' context only, with no tests for SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist or email_domains_blacklist paths. This is a legitimate testing gap for moved functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: | P2 | app/controllers/users_controller.rb:195 | The expanded failed-signup JSON contract and the client retry rejection behavior have no request or client test, so an error/value serialization mismatch would go undetected. | testing | high |

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new JSON response structure in users_controller.rb (lines 195-199) adding 'errors' and 'values' fields, and the corresponding client-side handling in create_account_controller.js (lines 271-274) that uses result.errors.email and result.values.email, lack integration tests. The diff shows new functionality where the server returns error details and the client uses them to track rejected emails, but no controller/integration tests are added to verify this contract. The spec files added only test the BlockedEmail model and EmailValidator in isolation, not the full request/response cycle.
